overview.text: The weak nuclear force, also called the weak interaction, is one of nature’s fundamental forces. Unlike the strong force, it does not bind protons and neutrons; instead, it can change a quark’s type, converting a neutron into a proton or vice versa. This makes it central to beta decay, in which a nucleus can change its number of protons and become a different element. The force is carried by the charged W boson and the neutral Z boson; their large masses give the interaction an extremely short range. It is also significant because electroweak theory connects the weak and electromagnetic forces as aspects of one interaction.

key_facts.text: In beta-minus decay, a neutron changes into a proton and the process produces an electron and an electron antineutrino.
The W boson carries electric charge; the Z boson is neutral.
The large masses of the W and Z bosons limit the weak force to an extremely short range—about 10⁻¹⁸ metres, according to CERN.
In the 1960s, Sheldon Glashow, Abdus Salam, and Steven Weinberg developed the theory connecting the weak and electromagnetic forces.
CERN reports that W and Z bosons were first observed in 1983, supporting a key part of the Standard Model.
